synopsis: TTC estimates the seconds until machine and object meet if neither changes speed, while trigger distance marks the decision to warn or brake; both depend on perceived range and relative speed [f12857, f12859]. Trigger distance includes travel during detection and decision, brake response, physical stopping, and a residual safe distance; a one-meter range error or speed estimate lag of a few tenths of a second changes TTC and the trigger point [f12858, f12860]. TTC alone is weak at work-site speeds, so the referenced standard and consensus favor stopping-distance and risk-zone logic with TTC as one input; an unnamed mining specification requests warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention, limiting traceability of that requirement [f12864, f12865, f12863]. Sensor-model validation should compare matched real and simulated TTC and trigger distance, with calibrated 3D reference labels when distance or TTC matters [f12867, f5402]. Across system comparison and campaign evaluation, the corpus recommends common ground truth and hazard zones, warning TTC, and verdicts extending beyond collisions to detection, intervention, stopping margin, nuisance effects and operator-warning sequence; scenario search can deliberately worsen TTC or other robustness measures to expose failures [f106, f7373, f6835].
